chapter_theme: At the Buddha's seat on Manipallavam the Manimekala goddess descends, praises the Buddha, and tells Manimekalai her former birth: as Lakshmi she fed a sky-roaming sage, a gift that will end her births; the prince who pursues her is her husband of that birth, Rahulan, and her sisters then are Madhavi and Sudhamathi now, reborn beside her for worshipping the Buddha's footprints; the goddess gives her a mantra to change form and fly, for hearing the false words of other schools, and one against hunger, since the body is a lump of food.

cast.role: Madhavi's daughter, who has just learned her former birth as Lakshmi
the sea goddess who carried Manimekalai to Manipallavam
the Buddha, whose seat stands on Manipallavam
Lakshmi's husband in that birth, reborn as Udayakumaran
a sky-roaming sage who took food from Lakshmi's hands
Lakshmi's elder sister, reborn as Madhavi
Lakshmi's elder sister, reborn as Sudhamathi
king of Kachchayam in Anga country, husband of Tharai and Veerai
the learned sage of Lakshmi's age who leads Thuchayan to the hill of the Buddha's footprints

manimekalai:10:1-15.reading: Knowing that the girl has recovered her former birth at the Buddha's seat, the Manimekala goddess comes down through the sky with fragrant flowers and, while Manimekalai stands listening, praises the Buddha as a young sun that rose when the world had lost its understanding and dharma's light had failed, bows to the seat as his own presence, and asks that her grief end.
manimekalai:10:1-15.nuance: The hymn (7 to 15) is read here as the goddess's, since she has just descended and the next unit has her circling the seat; the Tamil does not name the singer, and it could be Manimekalai's own prayer heard by the goddess. The seat is worshipped as the Buddha himself (நீயே ஆகி நிற்கு அமைந்த இவ் ஆசனம்): no image, only the place where he sat. Lines 1 and 2 seem to be the goddess's own thought before she descends.
manimekalai:10:1-15.event: The Manimekala goddess descends to Manipallavam and sings praise of the Buddha before his seat as Manimekalai listens.

claims.claim: the Buddha appeared to make dharma flourish in a world that had lost understanding, as a sun rises on darkness

manimekalai:10:16-39.reading: As the goddess circles and bows to the seat, Manimekalai falls at her feet, thanks her for the knowledge of her birth and asks where her husband is; the goddess recalls how Lakshmi, sulking with Rahulan in a grove, saw the sky-roaming sage Saadhusakkaran come down at noon from turning the wheel of dharma in Ratnadvipa, bowed in awe, silenced her angry husband for not bowing, and with him offered the sage water and food, which he accepted.
manimekalai:10:16-39.nuance: The scene is a lovers' quarrel (புலத்தகை, இடங்கழி காமம்) broken into by a holy man: Lakshmi turns from her husband's pleading at her feet to the sage's feet, and it is she, not Rahulan, who knows whom to honour. The sage calls her எம் அனை, 'my mother', as he accepts.
manimekalai:10:16-39.event: Manimekalai asks the goddess where her former husband is; the goddess tells how Lakshmi and Rahulan once fed the sage Saadhusakkaran in a grove.

manimekalai:10:40-49.unit_note: Boundary moved from 51 to 49: the goddess's account of the gift and the prince closes with செய்தேன் at 49; lines 50 and 51 open the sentence about Lakshmi's sisters, which runs to கொண்டனன் at 54.
manimekalai:10:40-49.reading: The goddess says that the charity the sage ate that day will not stay idle but will cut off Lakshmi's births, that Udayakumaran who came to her in the Uvavanam grove is that same Rahulan, and that because her heart too still clings to him, she carried her away, a seed of dharma about to fall like fine paddy seed on scorched saline ground, to set her on the right path.
manimekalai:10:40-49.nuance: This explains Manimekalai's own pull toward the prince and the goddess's taking her to the island: the gift's merit is secure, but a love that survives rebirth threatens to waste it. The goddess does not condemn the love as sin; she calls it the wrong ground for the seed.
manimekalai:10:40-49.event: The goddess reveals that Udayakumaran is Manimekalai's former husband Rahulan and that she carried her off to save the merit of her past gift.

claims.claim: food given to a holy one does not go to waste but will in time cut off the giver's rebirths
a love carried over from a former birth can waste the merit one has earned, as seed is lost on saline ground

manimekalai:10:50-70.unit_note: Boundary moved from 52 to 50: the sentence naming Lakshmi's sisters begins at 50 (இன்னும் கேளாய் இலக்குமி) and reaches its verb at 54.
manimekalai:10:50-70.reading: The goddess goes on: Lakshmi's elder sisters Tharai and Veerai were taken by Thuchayan, king of Kachchayam in Anga, and as he sported with them by the Ganga the flawless sage Aravanan came by; asked who he was, the sage said he had come to circle and worship the hill named for the lotus feet of the first lord of the dharma wheel, who once stood there and taught dharma with a melting heart so that people's sorrow and even the beasts' fear of one another might end, and he bade them worship too.
manimekalai:10:50-70.nuance: The goddess quotes Aravanan's speech inside her own, so 61 to 70 is a report two removes deep. The footprints are said to destroy faults (குற்றம் கெடுக்கும், 66) by lying there, which gives the place, not a living teacher, the power. Whether this Aravanan is the Aravana Adigal of Puhar in the story's present the unit does not say.
manimekalai:10:50-70.event: King Thuchayan, sporting with Tharai and Veerai by the Ganga, meets the sage Aravanan, who bids them worship the hill of the Buddha's footprints.

claims.claim: the first lord of the dharma wheel taught out of compassion that all living things, beasts too, should live together without fear
the Buddha's footprints on the hill destroy the faults of those who worship them

manimekalai:10:71-93.reading: Because the two sisters heeded the sage and worshipped at the hill, the goddess says, they have been reborn with Manimekalai as Madhavi and Sudhamathi; now that she knows her birth and dharma's worth she will hear the false teachings of many schools, and since no one will tell a young girl the truth, she gives her a mantra to change form and travel the sky, foretells the great sage's day on the full moon, tells her to worship the seat and go home, then turns back for something forgotten: the human body is a lump of food, and this second mantra cuts off hunger; then she rises and is gone.
manimekalai:10:71-93.nuance: Two mantras are given: one for changing form and flying, for hearing the schools in disguise (fulfilled in kaathai 27), and one against hunger, added as an afterthought (மறந்ததும் உண்டு). The goddess calls the other schools' teachings படிற்று உரை, false or deceitful words, before Manimekalai has heard them. Lines 83 to 85 are obscure: the full-moon day on which the great sage 'attains holy dharma' may be the Buddha's festival or a prophecy about Manimekalai's own path.
manimekalai:10:71-93.event: The goddess tells Manimekalai that her sisters of the former birth are Madhavi and Sudhamathi, gives her a mantra for changing form and flying and another against hunger, and departs into the sky.

claims.claim: worship of the Buddha's footprints in one birth brings its fruit in the next, as rebirth beside the one who led the way
the teachings of the various other schools are false words
the human body is a lump made of food, so hunger rules it

links.note: The goddess foretells that Manimekalai will hear the false words of the many schools and gives her a mantra to take another form; in kaathai 27 she goes among the reckoners of Vanji in an ascetic's borrowed form and questions them one by one.
links.teaches: The debate chapter is set up as a test prepared for in advance: the disguise exists because the goddess expects no one to tell a young girl the truth, so the schools are heard under a mask chosen against their condescension.

links.note: Sudhamathi's sermon on the body born of deeds failed to turn Udayakumaran once he saw Manimekalai; the goddess now reveals that he is her husband of a former birth and that her heart, too, still clings to him.
links.teaches: The failure of the grove sermon is given a cause in karma after the fact: the pull between the two was not mere sight but a bond carried across births, which is why words could not break it and a goddess had to carry her away.

links.note: The akam heroine asks that, when this life turns into the next, the same man be her husband and she the one close to his heart; the goddess tells Manimekalai that exactly this has come about, her heart still bound to her former husband, and calls it seed falling on scorched saline ground.
links.teaches: The bond across births that the akam poem asks for as the highest pledge of love is, in the Buddhist epic, the very danger to the merit that would end births, so the same wish is fulfilled and judged a loss.

gains.a: The goddess's verdict is seen to overturn a fixed ideal of Tamil love poetry, not just a passing desire of the prince.
gains.b: The heroine's vow gets a sequel in which it is granted, and its cost, the turning of rebirth into a trap, is shown.

links.note: The quatrain says a small act of virtue that reaches worthy hands spreads like a banyan from a tiny seed; the goddess says Lakshmi's meal to a sage will not go to waste but will cut off her births, and also that the giver herself, as a seed of dharma, could be lost on barren ground.
links.teaches: The epic agrees that a gift to the worthy grows, but changes its harvest from a covering shade of merit to the end of rebirth, and adds that the giver's own attachments can still waste what the gift has sown.

gains.a: The goddess's claim at 41 is placed within an ethics-book teaching on giving to the worthy, which marks how far its promised fruit goes beyond that teaching.
gains.b: The quatrain's growth image is shown to depend on the giver as well as the receiver, a condition it does not state.

links.note: Tirumular bids the seeker hold to the Lord's feet, by whom strong deeds perish, and says the Lord will set him among the gods; Aravanan calls the Buddha's footprints on the hill the feet that destroy faults, and the next unit says the sisters who worshipped there were reborn beside Lakshmi.
links.teaches: Both give the feet power over past deeds, but the Saiva feet belong to a Lord who acts now and places the soul, while the Buddhist feet are the trace of a teacher who left long ago, and their fruit comes from the worshippers' own act ripening in the next birth.

gains.a: The footprint hill is seen as a Buddhist answer to the feet-devotion of Tamil theism, with the giver of grace replaced by a place and a remembered teaching.
gains.b: The verse's agent, the Lord who sets the soul among the gods, stands out as the thing a rival tradition does without while keeping the image of the feet.

links.note: Kudapulaviyanar tells the Pandya that food makes the body (உண்டி முதற்றே உணவின் பிண்டம்), so those who bind water to land give body and life, and bids him build tanks; the goddess uses the same phrase, the body is a lump of food, to give Manimekalai a mantra that cuts off her own hunger.
links.teaches: The same maxim drives two answers to hunger: the Sangam poet makes it a king's duty to feed a people by irrigation, the epic turns it into an ascetic's private release from hunger, the first step before the bowl that will feed others.

gains.a: The goddess's sudden afterthought at 90 is heard as a known saying about kings and food, which foreshadows Manimekalai's later role as feeder of the hungry.
gains.b: The poem's maxim is shown carried from the king's public works to a single renouncer's body, where the remedy is a mantra, not water.

links.note: The couplet ranks the strength of enduring hunger below the strength of removing others' hunger; the goddess gives Manimekalai the first strength by mantra, and the patikam (manimekalai:0:51-68) says the bowl for feeding others comes next.
links.teaches: The epic follows the couplet's order of rank but removes the effort from the lower strength: enduring hunger is granted as a gift, so the renouncer is freed for the higher task the couplet values, feeding others.

gains.a: The hunger mantra is seen as a step in a known scale of virtue rather than a magic convenience.
gains.b: The couplet's ranking is shown worked out in a life, where the lesser strength is a means to the greater rather than a rival to it.

source_issues: Line 40 carries the line mark 110-040 with kaathai number 110; read as 10-040.
Line 7 opens the hymn with a single quotation mark and line 15 closes it with a double one; the speaker is not named.
Line 87 has a quotation mark before பதிப் புகுவாய் inside a speech opened at 83, leaving the goddess's quoted speech unbalanced.
Line 93 ends with a bare என், the kaathai's closing particle, so the last sentence reads as cut short in this text.
